newsitem.title: INDIA: Rescuers find 24 dead from India train explosion.
newsitem.headline: Rescuers find 24 dead from India train explosion.

text.p: Rescuers recovered 24 bodies by daybreak on Tuesday from a packed train ripped by a bomb planted by suspected separatist guerrillas in northeastern India, and officials said the toll could rise sharply.

Three of the train's 15 carriages -- each crammed with 75 to 100 people going off on holiday -- were destroyed in the blast after the train left Kokrajhar station in Assam state for Delhi around 7 p.m. (1330 GMT) on Monday, police said.
Soon after the explosion, a senior police officer in Assam's capital Guwahati said at least 300 people were believed dead.

But darkness and the remoteness of the region hampered rescuers and compounded confusion over the number of dead and wounded. As day broke, 24 bodies, including those of 10 children, had been found in the mangled wreckage.

"They have recovered 24 dead and 63 injured," a police official in Guwahati told Reuters by telephone, quoting rescuers at the site of the blast in Sensapani, 200 km (125 miles) west of the state capital.
He said it would not be clear until later in the day whether at least 300 people had died, as police earlier said.
Asked if the death toll was expected to rise, the official said: "It could. Rescue and recovery operations are on. They are looking for more dead bodies."
Asked if authorities would confirm the earlier estimate of at least 300 dead, the police official said: "It is guesswork."
There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the attack, which authorities blamed on Bodo tribal guerrillas who have waged a separatist struggle for nearly a decade.
Police said militants had used a remote-controlled device to blow up the Delhi-bound Brahmaputra Mail, an express train named after the sacred river that flows through India's northeast.
At least 1,000 people were travelling on the train, according to officials. Most of the passengers were believed to be holidaymakers heading for Delhi to celebrate the New Year.
Sensapani is seven km (four miles) west of Kokrajhar, a centre of Bodo separatist activity.
The Bodos are one of many indigenous tribes in hilly northeastern India and among dozens of groups waging separatist campaigns across the country.
The animist Bodos have been demanding a separate tribal state north of the Brahmaputra river since the early 1980s, and their campaign took a violent turn at the end of the decade.
At least 1,000 had died in violence related to the Bodo struggle for independence, United News of India said.

One of the coaches torn apart by the blast was an air-conditioned carriage with reserved seats. Another was for passengers without reservations and was thought to be carrying far more than its capacity.
The third carriage was a restaurant car, and railway officials said an explosion of cooking gas cylinders could have caused more deaths.
Police and residents of Kokrajhar town said they heard at least two explosions. One police official said a series of devices might have been detonated on the train track.
